scenarios.title: Fixing the Bus Saathi Ticket Screen
scenarios.background: Bus Saathi is a fictional city-bus app in Bhopal used by students, office workers and elderly riders. The home screen shows eight items with equal weight, and 'Buy ticket' is a small grey link among them. The body text is light grey on white. After a rider taps 'Pay', nothing changes on screen for about five seconds, so many riders tap again and are charged twice. The new design intern has been asked to fix the screen using standard design principles.
constraints: Many riders use the app outdoors in bright sunlight
Riders range from teenagers to people in their seventies
The app must keep working on small, low-cost phones

questions.prompt: Most riders open the app to buy a ticket, but they struggle to find the small grey 'Buy ticket' link. What should the intern change?

options.text: Add an animated banner that says 'Tickets available here'
Make 'Buy ticket' the largest, highest-contrast button on top
Move 'Buy ticket' into a menu that opens from a hamburger icon
Give all eight home-screen items the same bright orange colour

questions.explanation: Visual hierarchy guides attention through size, contrast and position, so the most frequent task should be the most prominent thing on the screen. Making 'Buy ticket' a large, high-contrast primary button near the top lets riders find it at a glance.

why_others_wrong.a: A banner adds noise and moving distraction while the actual action stays small and hard to tap.
why_others_wrong.c: Hiding the main task in a menu makes it harder to find, not easier.
why_others_wrong.d: When everything is emphasised equally, nothing stands out, which is the current problem.

questions.key_justification: Give the primary task the strongest visual weight on the screen.

questions.prompt: Riders cannot read the light grey body text outdoors. What is the right standard to apply?

options.text: A contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 for normal-size body text
Any grey text is acceptable as long as the font is a modern one
Make the text lighter still, so the whole screen looks cleaner
Use a contrast ratio of about 2:1 to keep a soft, calm feeling

questions.explanation: WCAG level AA asks for a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 between normal-size text and its background, and 3:1 for large text. Meeting it makes text readable for people with weaker eyesight and in bright sunlight.

why_others_wrong.b: A typeface does not fix low contrast; the colours still need enough difference.
why_others_wrong.c: Lighter text lowers contrast further and makes the problem worse.
why_others_wrong.d: 2:1 is well below the accessibility minimum and is unreadable for many people outdoors.

questions.key_justification: Body text needs at least 4.5:1 contrast to meet WCAG AA.

questions.prompt: After tapping 'Pay', nothing happens for five seconds and riders pay twice. Which two changes fix this?

options.text: Show a clear 'Processing payment' state right after the tap
Add a second confirmation pop-up after the payment completes
Disable the Pay button once it is tapped until the result arrives
Hide the ticket price so that riders feel less anxious about it
Change the Pay button's colour every second while riders wait

questions.explanation: Immediate feedback tells riders their tap worked, which is the heuristic of making system status visible. Disabling the button while the payment is in progress prevents the duplicate tap outright, which is error prevention.

why_others_wrong.b: A pop-up after completion comes too late; the double tap has already happened.
why_others_wrong.d: Hiding the price removes information riders need and does nothing about the double payment.
why_others_wrong.e: A flashing button looks broken or alarming and invites more taps.

questions.key_justification: Show system status immediately and prevent errors by blocking duplicate submissions.

questions.prompt: Match each design choice to the usability heuristic it follows.

items.text: A back arrow lets riders leave a wrong route screen at once
Labels say 'bus stop' rather than technical words like 'node'
The 'Buy' button looks and behaves the same on every screen
Recent stops are listed so riders do not have to type them again

targets.text: Match between the system and the real world

questions.explanation: An easy way out of a wrong screen gives riders control and freedom. Everyday words match how riders think about the real world, a button that behaves the same everywhere follows consistency, and showing recent stops lets riders recognise an option instead of recalling and typing it.

why_others_wrong.common_mistake: Calling the recent stops list 'consistency': the point is that riders pick from what they see instead of remembering it, which is recognition rather than recall.

questions.key_justification: Each choice applies a different one of Nielsen's usability heuristics.

scenarios.title: Researching Saheli Before Designing It
scenarios.background: Saheli is a fictional health information app for women in smaller towns of Madhya Pradesh and Chhattisgarh. It has 60 articles, a period tracker and paid video consultations with doctors. Many people install it, but most leave during sign-up, and nobody on the team knows why. The founders have strong opinions about what users want, but the team has never spoken to them directly. A new UX designer has six weeks and a small research budget.
constraints: Users are reached mostly through local health workers
Health topics are sensitive, so research must be private and respectful
The budget covers sessions with about ten participants

questions.prompt: The team does not know why most people leave during sign-up. What is the best first research step?

options.text: Send a survey to 5,000 users asking them to rate sign-up out of ten
Ask the founders why they think people are leaving at sign-up
Watch five target users try to sign up while thinking aloud
Redesign the sign-up flow with no research and compare numbers

questions.explanation: Watching a handful of real users attempt the task while they think aloud shows exactly where and why they get stuck. Around five participants usually uncover most of the major problems in a single flow, which fits the budget.

why_others_wrong.a: A rating shows that people are unhappy, not what confuses them or where.
why_others_wrong.b: Founders' guesses are exactly the assumptions research is meant to test.
why_others_wrong.d: Redesigning without understanding the cause is likely to repeat or replace the problem.

questions.key_justification: Use a small think-aloud usability test to find why users fail a task.

questions.prompt: Which interview question will give the most honest, useful answer?

options.text: 'Wouldn't you love an app that tracks every symptom for you?'
'Tell me about the last time you looked for health advice.'
'Do you agree that our period tracker is easy to use?'
'How much would you pay each month for our video consultations?'

questions.explanation: An open question about a real past event lets the participant describe what actually happened in her own words, revealing needs and habits the team had not imagined. It avoids suggesting an answer or asking her to predict the future.

why_others_wrong.a: This leads the participant toward 'yes', so her answer reflects politeness more than need.
why_others_wrong.c: Asking for agreement invites people to say what the interviewer seems to want.
why_others_wrong.d: People are poor at predicting what they would pay, and the question puts them on the spot.

questions.key_justification: Ask open, non-leading questions about real past behaviour.

questions.prompt: The team wants the 60 articles grouped in a way that makes sense to users. Which method fits best?

options.text: Group them by the departments the company's doctors work in
Put all 60 articles in alphabetical order on a single long list
Copy the menu structure that a large hospital's website uses
Run a card sort where target users group the article topics

questions.explanation: In a card sort, participants group topic cards in the way that makes sense to them and often name the groups, which reveals their mental model. The menu can then be built around the groupings users actually expect.

why_others_wrong.a: Medical departments reflect the company's structure, not how users think about their health questions.
why_others_wrong.b: A 60-item alphabetical list forces users to know the exact title they want.
why_others_wrong.c: A hospital website serves different users and goals, so its structure may not fit these users.

questions.key_justification: Card sorting reveals users' mental models for organising content.

questions.prompt: The team wants personas to guide design decisions. Which two qualities make a persona useful?

options.text: It is based on patterns seen in real interviews and data
It is invented in a brainstorm, with a stock photo and hobbies
It describes her goals, frustrations and the context she lives in
It tries to describe every possible user in one single profile
It reflects the CEO's personal idea of who the ideal user is

questions.explanation: A persona is only as good as the evidence behind it, so it should summarise patterns seen across real participants. Its goals, frustrations and context, such as sharing one phone with family, are what help the team decide between design options.

why_others_wrong.b: A made-up persona encodes the team's assumptions instead of real users.
why_others_wrong.d: A persona that describes everyone guides no decision.
why_others_wrong.e: One person's view is an assumption, not research.

questions.key_justification: Useful personas are evidence-based and capture goals, pain points and context.

questions.prompt: Match each research question to the method that answers it best.

items.text: Which of two sign-up button labels gets more completed sign-ups?
Where in the menu do users expect to find the period tracker?
How do daily routines shape when women look for health advice?
Can a first-time user book a video consultation without help?

targets.text: A diary study over two weeks
An A/B test with live traffic
A tree test of the menu structure

questions.explanation: Comparing two labels on real behaviour needs an A/B test with enough traffic. A tree test checks whether people can find items in a proposed menu, a diary study captures habits over time in daily life, and a usability test shows whether a first-time user can complete a task.

why_others_wrong.common_mistake: Using a usability test to choose between button labels: five participants cannot show which label produces more sign-ups, which needs an A/B test at scale.

questions.key_justification: Match the method to whether the question is about behaviour at scale, findability, context or task success.

code_pool.prompt: Most people leave Saheli during sign-up and nobody knows why, so the team ran usability tests. Summarise them. The first line is n, then n sessions `participant task outcome seconds` (outcome success, fail or abandon). Complete `task_results`: per task, sorted by name, the success rate as a whole percent rounded down, and the median time of the successful attempts only (the mean of the two middle values when there is an even number), to one decimal, or `-` if nobody succeeded. The program prints `task pct% median`.
code_pool.starter_code:
import sys


def task_results(sessions):
    """sessions: (participant, task, success|fail|abandon, seconds). Per task, sorted by task: the success rate as a whole percent rounded down, and the median time of the SUCCESSFUL attempts (the mean of the two middle values for an even count), or None if nobody succeeded. Return [(task, pct, median)]."""
    # Write your code here.
    return []


def main():
    data = sys.stdin.read().split("\n")
    n = int(data[0])
    sessions = []
    for i in range(n):
        participant, task, outcome, seconds = data[1 + i].split()
        sessions.append((participant, task, outcome, int(seconds)))
    for task, pct, median in task_results(sessions):
        print(task, f"{pct}%", "-" if median is None else format(median, ".1f"))


main()
code_pool.explanation: Grouping sessions by task gives the completion rate, the first number in any usability report. The median time is used rather than the mean because one participant who got stuck for minutes would drag a mean far away from the typical experience; and only successful attempts count, since a give-up time is not a task time.
code_pool.key_justification: Group by task; success rate and median of successful times.

code_pool.prompt: Before redesigning Saheli's menus, participants sorted topic cards into piles that made sense to them (an open card sort). Find the groups they agree on. The first line is `participants threshold` (threshold as a percent), the second is n, then n piles `participant pile_name card,card,...`. Complete `card_clusters`: two cards are linked when at least threshold% of participants put them in the same pile; clusters are connected groups of linked cards, and a card with no links is a cluster of its own. The program prints each cluster as `card, card` (sorted), clusters ordered by their first card.
code_pool.starter_code:
import sys


def card_clusters(groups, participants, threshold):
    """groups: (participant, [cards in one pile]). Two cards are linked when at least `threshold` percent of participants put them in the same pile. Clusters are the connected groups of linked cards (a card with no links is a cluster on its own). Return clusters, each sorted, ordered by their first card."""
    # Write your code here.
    return [[c] for _, pile in groups for c in pile]


def main():
    data = sys.stdin.read().split("\n")
    participants, threshold = map(int, data[0].split())
    n = int(data[1])
    groups = []
    for i in range(n):
        participant, _, cards = data[2 + i].split()
        groups.append((participant, cards.split(",")))
    for cluster in card_clusters(groups, participants, threshold):
        print(", ".join(cluster))


main()
code_pool.explanation: Counting, for every pair of cards, how many people piled them together gives a similarity matrix; keeping strong pairs as edges and taking connected components turns it into the menu groups users expect. It replaces the founders' opinions with evidence of how users think.
code_pool.key_justification: Pair co-occurrence, then connected components in a graph.

scenarios.title: Why Farmers Abandon the Kisan Rin Loan Form
scenarios.background: Kisan Rin is a fictional crop-loan app from a co-operative bank in Maharashtra. Analytics show that 60% of applicants abandon the loan form, which has 25 fields on one long screen. Error messages appear only after submitting, in a red banner at the top of the page. 'Submit' and 'Cancel' sit next to each other as small buttons, and the bottom navigation uses icons with no labels. Support calls come mostly from farmers over fifty, and many apply outdoors.
constraints: Some fields are legally required for the loan
Many applicants have little experience with apps
The form must work on small phone screens

questions.prompt: Most applicants quit the 25-field form on its single long screen. What should the designer try first?

options.text: Make every field smaller so the whole form fits on one phone screen
Split it into short steps with a progress bar, asking only what is needed
Add a pop-up that warns applicants how long the form is going to take
Remove some legally required fields to make the form shorter for all

def funnel(steps):
    """steps: (step, people who reached it), in form order. kept = reached / previous step's reached x 100 (the first step is 100). Return ([(step, reached, kept)], (step with the biggest drop = 100 - kept, that drop)), the earliest step on a tie; the first step never counts as a drop."""

    return [(s, r, 100.0) for s, r in steps], (steps[-1][0], 0.0)


def main():

    steps = []
    for i in range(n):
        name, reached = data[1 + i].split()
        steps.append((name, int(reached)))
    rows, worst = funnel(steps)
    for name, reached, kept in rows:
        print(name, reached, format(kept, ".1f") + "%")
    print("biggest_drop", worst[0], format(worst[1], ".1f") + "%")


main()

def funnel(steps):
    """steps: (step, people who reached it), in form order. kept = reached / previous step's reached x 100 (the first step is 100). Return ([(step, reached, kept)], (step with the biggest drop = 100 - kept, that drop)), the earliest step on a tie; the first step never counts as a drop."""
    rows, worst = [], None
    for i, (name, reached) in enumerate(steps):
        kept = 100.0 if i == 0 else 100 * reached / steps[i - 1][1]   # relative to the step before
        rows.append((name, reached, kept))
        if i and (worst is None or 100 - kept > worst[1]):

    return rows, worst


def main():

    n = int(data[0])
    steps = []
    for i in range(n):
        name, reached = data[1 + i].split()

    rows, worst = funnel(steps)
    for name, reached, kept in rows:
        print(name, reached, format(kept, ".1f") + "%")
    print("biggest_drop", worst[0], format(worst[1], ".1f") + "%")


main()

import re
import sys


def check_field(field, value):
    """Return None if valid, else the friendly message. name: not empty -> 'Enter your name'. aadhaar: 12 digits (spaces allowed between them) -> 'Aadhaar must be 12 digits'. mobile: 10 digits starting with 6-9 -> 'Mobile must be 10 digits starting with 6, 7, 8 or 9'. ifsc: 4 capital letters, a 0, then 6 capital letters or digits -> 'IFSC looks like SBIN0001234'. acres: a number above 0 with at most 2 decimals -> 'Enter land in acres, like 2.5'."""
    rules = {
        "name": (lambda v: v != "", "Enter your name"),
        "aadhaar": (lambda v: re.fullmatch(r"[0-9]{12}", v.replace(" ", "")), "Aadhaar must be 12 digits"),
        "mobile": (lambda v: re.fullmatch(r"[6-9][0-9]{9}", v), "Mobile must be 10 digits starting with 6, 7, 8 or 9"),
        "ifsc": (lambda v: re.fullmatch(r"[A-Z]{4}0[A-Z0-9]{6}", v), "IFSC looks like SBIN0001234"),
        "acres": (lambda v: re.fullmatch(r"[0-9]+(\.[0-9]{1,2})?", v) and float(v) > 0, "Enter land in acres, like 2.5"),
    }
    check, message = rules[field]
    return None if check(value) else message


def main():
    data = sys.stdin.read().split("\n")
    n = int(data[0])
    for i in range(n):
        field, _, value = data[1 + i].partition(" ")
        message = check_field(field, value.strip())
        print(field, "OK" if message is None else "- " + message)


main()
code_pool.explanation: Each field gets a precise rule (a small pattern) and a message that says how to fix it, shown next to that field as soon as it is filled. Accepting spaces in an Aadhaar number, as people write it on the card, is kinder than rejecting it; the rule should fit the user, not the database.
code_pool.key_justification: Field validation with patterns and actionable messages.

scenarios.title: Business Goals and Users' Trust at Bachat Bank
scenarios.background: Bachat Bank is a fictional digital bank in Kolkata with six product teams, each designing its own screens. The result is three different button styles and two date pickers. Marketing wants a pre-ticked 'Add accident insurance for 99 rupees a month' box on the account-opening screen and fewer visible fee details 'to keep the screen clean'. The app is launching in six Indian languages next quarter, and leadership asks the design lead to balance growth targets with customers' trust.
constraints: Banking regulators expect clear disclosure of fees
Six teams ship changes every two weeks
The app must work in six languages, including scripts with taller characters

questions.prompt: Marketing wants the insurance add-on box pre-ticked when customers open an account. What should the design lead recommend?

options.text: Pre-tick it, as most people will not notice and revenue goes up
Leave it unticked, explain the cost and benefit, and let them opt in
Pre-tick it but put the monthly price in small grey text below
Pre-tick it and only let customers remove it by calling support

questions.explanation: A pre-ticked paid add-on relies on people not noticing, which is a dark pattern that breaks trust and invites complaints. An unticked box with a clear explanation of price and benefit means everyone who buys it chose it, which is fairer to customers and safer for the bank.

why_others_wrong.a: Revenue from customers who did not notice turns into refunds, complaints and lost trust.
why_others_wrong.c: Hiding the price in faint text makes the dark pattern worse.
why_others_wrong.d: Making removal hard adds a second dark pattern on top of the first.

questions.key_justification: Avoid dark patterns; paid add-ons should be clear, unticked opt-ins.

questions.prompt: Six teams have produced three button styles and two date pickers. What is the best long-term fix?

options.text: Let each team keep its own style so it can move as fast as it likes
Have one designer review and redraw every screen from every team
Build a shared design system of tokens and documented components
Freeze all design changes until every screen in the app matches

questions.explanation: A design system gives every team the same colours, type, spacing and documented components, so consistency comes from reuse rather than policing. It takes upfront effort, but each team then ships faster because common pieces are already designed and built.

why_others_wrong.a: Inconsistent controls confuse customers and multiply the work of maintaining the app.
why_others_wrong.b: One reviewer becomes a bottleneck for six teams shipping every two weeks.
why_others_wrong.d: Freezing all changes stops the product from improving.

questions.key_justification: Shared, documented components and tokens scale consistency across teams.

questions.prompt: Marketing wants fee details removed from the transfer confirmation screen to keep it minimal. What should the design lead do?

options.text: Remove the fees entirely, as a clean screen converts more customers
Show fees only after the money has already been transferred
Move the fees into a help article that is linked from the footer
Show the fee and total clearly before confirming, styled simply

questions.explanation: Customers need to know what a transfer will cost before agreeing to it, and regulators expect fees to be disclosed clearly. Good layout and typography can keep the screen calm while still showing the fee and the total right before the confirm button.

why_others_wrong.a: Hiding costs damages trust and conflicts with disclosure expectations.
why_others_wrong.b: Showing the fee after the transfer is too late for the customer to decide.
why_others_wrong.c: Few customers read a footer help article before confirming a transfer.

questions.key_justification: Clarity about costs outweighs minimalism; disclose fees before confirmation.

questions.prompt: The app will launch in six Indian languages. Which two design practices prepare it best?

options.text: Design layouts that allow for longer and taller translated text
Fix every button's width to fit the English wording exactly
Review translations with native speakers in real screens
Machine-translate every screen and ship it without a review
Put the interface text inside images to keep fonts consistent

questions.explanation: Translated text is often longer than English, and some scripts need more line height, so flexible layouts prevent clipped or overlapping labels. Native speakers reviewing text in context catch awkward or wrong translations, especially for financial terms.

why_others_wrong.b: English-sized buttons cut off longer translations.
why_others_wrong.d: Unreviewed machine translation of banking terms can confuse or mislead customers.
why_others_wrong.e: Text in images cannot be translated, resized or read by screen readers.

questions.key_justification: Localisation needs flexible layouts and native-speaker review in context.

import sys


def luminance(colour):
    channels = []
    for i in (1, 3, 5):                                   # 'RR', 'GG', 'BB' after the '#'
        c = int(colour[i:i + 2], 16) / 255
        channels.append(c / 12.92 if c <= 0.04045 else ((c + 0.055) / 1.055) ** 2.4)
    r, g, b = channels
    return 0.2126 * r + 0.7152 * g + 0.0722 * b


def contrast_ratio(fg, bg):
    """fg, bg: colours '#RRGGBB'. WCAG: each channel c = value / 255, made linear as c / 12.92 if c <= 0.04045 else ((c + 0.055) / 1.055) ** 2.4; luminance L = 0.2126 R + 0.7152 G + 0.0722 B; ratio = (lighter L + 0.05) / (darker L + 0.05)."""
    a, b = luminance(fg), luminance(bg)
    lighter, darker = max(a, b), min(a, b)
    return (lighter + 0.05) / (darker + 0.05)


def main():
    data = sys.stdin.read().split("\n")
    n = int(data[0])
    for i in range(n):
        fg, bg = data[1 + i].split()
        r = contrast_ratio(fg, bg)
        print(f"{fg} {bg} ratio {r:.2f} normal", "PASS" if r >= 4.5 else "FAIL", "large", "PASS" if r >= 3 else "FAIL")


main()

scenarios.title: Redesigning the Sahaj Nagrik Citizen App
scenarios.background: Sahaj Nagrik is a fictional citizen-services app for a state government, used to apply for income and caste certificates, pay property tax and track applications. Usage is low, and most people still queue at offices. Users range from college students to elderly people with low literacy, and some rely on screen readers. Every department wants its own link on the home screen, and the deadline is tight. The design lead must run a redesign from research to developer handoff.
constraints: Users include people with low literacy and people using screen readers
Twelve departments each want visibility on the home screen
The launch date is fixed by the government

questions.prompt: Put the stages of the redesign in order.

options.text: Sketch and explore several possible solutions
Research citizens' needs, tasks and context
Test the prototype with citizens and iterate
Define the core problems and success measures
Build an interactive prototype of the best idea

questions.explanation: Research comes first so the team understands real needs, and those findings are turned into a clear problem and success measures. The team then explores several ideas, prototypes the most promising, and tests it with citizens, repeating as needed.

why_others_wrong.common_mistake: Sketching solutions before defining the problem, which leads the team to polish ideas that solve the wrong thing.

questions.key_justification: Research, define, ideate, prototype, then test and iterate.

questions.prompt: How should the team judge whether the redesign succeeded?

options.text: Count how many screens the new design has compared with the old
Ask the department heads whether the new design looks modern
Measure task completion and time for top tasks, before and after
Count how many likes the launch announcement gets on social media

questions.explanation: The goal is for citizens to finish real tasks such as applying for a certificate. Measuring completion rate and time on those tasks in usability tests and in analytics, before and after the redesign, shows whether it actually helped.

why_others_wrong.a: Fewer or more screens says nothing about whether citizens can finish their tasks.
why_others_wrong.b: Officials' taste is not evidence of usability for citizens.
why_others_wrong.d: Likes measure the announcement's reach, not whether the app works for people.

questions.key_justification: Measure design success by task success for real users.

questions.prompt: What should the handoff to developers include?

options.text: Only the polished main screens, exported as flat PNG images
Design-system components with every state, such as empty and error
A short verbal walkthrough, leaving developers to fill in the rest
The full research notes, so developers can work out the screens

questions.explanation: Developers build what is specified, so screens need their loading, empty, error and success states, not just the happy path. Using shared components with annotations on behaviour and accessibility, such as focus order and labels, lets them build it consistently.

why_others_wrong.a: Flat images miss states, spacing values and interactions, so developers have to guess.
why_others_wrong.c: A verbal walkthrough is quickly forgotten and leaves most decisions undocumented.
why_others_wrong.d: Research explains why, but developers still need the specific designs and states.

questions.key_justification: Handoff should cover all states and reuse documented components with annotations.

questions.prompt: Some users have low literacy and some use screen readers. Which two choices serve them best?

options.text: Label every control and keep a logical focus order for screen readers
Show status using colour alone, such as green dots and red dots
Use plain, simple wording supported by clear icons and examples
Add a hard CAPTCHA puzzle to every single form submission screen
Use small text so that more information fits on every screen

questions.explanation: Proper labels and a logical focus order let screen-reader users understand and move through each screen. Plain language with supporting icons and examples helps people with low literacy understand what each step asks of them.

why_others_wrong.b: Colour alone fails for colour-blind and screen-reader users.
why_others_wrong.d: Hard CAPTCHAs block many users with disabilities and low literacy.
why_others_wrong.e: Small text is harder for everyone to read, especially older users.

questions.key_justification: Accessible services need proper semantics for assistive technology and plain language.

questions.prompt: Match each stakeholder request to the best response.

items.text: 'We have no time for user testing before launch.'
'Every department needs its own link on the home screen.'
'Citizens will figure it out on their own eventually.'
'Just copy the design of a famous shopping app.'

targets.text: Show short recordings of citizens struggling with the app

def sus_score(answers):
    """answers: the 10 System Usability Scale answers, each 1-5, item 1 first. Odd-numbered items score answer - 1, even-numbered items score 5 - answer; the SUS score is the total x 2.5 (0-100)."""

    print("mean", format(sum(scores) / n, ".1f"))


main()

import sys


def menu_path(edges, target):
    """edges: (parent, child) pairs of a menu tree whose root is 'Home'. Return the list of labels from Home down to target, or None if target is not in the menu."""
    parent = {child: par for par, child in edges}     # each item has one parent in a tree
    if target != "Home" and target not in parent:
        return None
    path = [target]
    while path[-1] != "Home":                          # walk up to the root, then reverse
        path.append(parent[path[-1]])
    return path[::-1]


def main():
    data = sys.stdin.read().split("\n")
    n = int(data[0])
    edges = [tuple(data[1 + i].split()) for i in range(n)]
    m = int(data[1 + n])
    for i in range(m):
        target = data[2 + n + i].strip()
        path = menu_path(edges, target)
        if path is None:
            print(f"{target}: NOT FOUND")
        else:
            clicks = len(path) - 1
            print(f"{target}: {' > '.join(path)} (clicks {clicks})" + (" TOO DEEP" if clicks > 3 else ""))


main()
code_pool.explanation: In a tree every node has exactly one parent, so a child-to-parent dictionary lets you walk from any label up to the root and reverse the path: O(depth) per question. Depth is the number of taps; anything beyond three is where people give up and queue at the office instead.
code_pool.key_justification: Parent pointers in a tree; walk up to build the path.
